  • Do not let cards query controllers or mutate servers directly; all actions flow through existing state holders.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Shared operational components
docs.text:
1. Create status badges, connection cards, capability count cards, row overflow actions, and confirmation patterns.
  2. Standardize working, failed, disabled, and installed states across MCP, skills, tools, and sandbox setup.
  3. Add a dedicated empty state for each collection instead of a generic blank list.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Tools management page
docs.text:
1. Add a Tools Overview header that summarizes enabled native tools, connected MCP servers, and installed skills.
  2. Redesign MCP servers as cards with connection status, refresh time/status, enable switch, detail view, and remove action.
  3. Present Popular Servers as a separate discovery area, not mixed with active connections.
  4. Redesign Skills as installed and discoverable groups with installation progress and actionable error states.
  5. Keep Native Tools as a responsive card grid, but add grouping and search/filter when the collection is large.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Sandbox setup
docs.text:
1. Turn the current setup card into a readiness flow with environment explanation, storage/session expectations, selected distribution, and install progress.
  2. Make cancellation, retry, reset, and package installation status clear without burying error text.
  3. Link skills that require a sandbox to the setup flow using a clear prerequisite state.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Sandbox workspace
docs.text:
1. Give Terminal, Files, and Packages a common workspace header and shared navigation.
  2. On desktop, show session selection above or beside the terminal and keep Files/Packages available as supporting panes.
  3. On compact layouts, retain the tab model with larger targets and selected-tab visibility.
  4. Present terminal sessions as named, stateful tabs with active/running status and close action.
  5. Keep terminal, file, and package controls independently scrollable and keyboard accessible.

docs.title: Phase 5 — Accessibility, safety, and validation
docs.text:
1. Give every stateful control an accessible name and state description.
  2. Require an explicit confirmation UI before reset, removal, or other irreversible environment actions.
  3. Validate touch targets, focus flow, large fonts, terminal contrast, and keyboard navigation.
  4. Add screenshot cases for disconnected, connected, installing, error, sandbox setup, multiple sessions, files, and packages.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• Users can see the difference between a tool that is available, enabled, connected, installing, or failed.
  • MCP, skills, and native tools are manageable without entering the sandbox workspace.
  • Sandbox setup and operation are understandable at a glance on compact and desktop screens.
  • Existing controller/view-model ownership stays intact.
  • Destructive actions have explicit confirmation and existing undo behavior remains where supported.

docs.title: Risks and controls
docs.text:
• MCP and skill installation may be asynchronous. Every mutation must render a durable in-progress or error state from the view model.
  • Sandbox availability is platform-dependent. Keep capability flags in state and avoid platform checks inside shared cards.
  • Terminal performance and focus can regress if nested scroll or gesture handlers are added carelessly; keep the terminal pane isolated from surrounding scroll containers.

docs.title: Progress status
docs.text: All five phases are implemented, each compiled against the desktop target and committed separately.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Shared operational components (done)
docs.text:
• New ui/components/OperationalComponents.kt: OperationalStatus vocabulary (Connected / Connecting / Disabled / Installing / NeedsSetup / Error / Active / Ready), a shared status color ramp, StatusBadge (dot + text so status never rides on color alone), CapabilityCountCard, and CollectionEmptyState.
  • MCP server cards show a text status badge (including Disabled and Not checked, not just the four connection colors) and a dedicated empty state.
  • Skills show a Needs setup badge on the sandbox prerequisite plus an empty-state card; native tools use the empty-state card too.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Tools management page (done)
docs.text:
• Tools Overview header: count cards for enabled native tools (X / Y), connected MCP servers (X / Y), and installed skills, each with an attention/needs-setup status badge. Responsive 3/2/1-column layout.
  • Native tools gain a search/filter field when the collection has 8+ items; localized display names are resolved first so localized names match. No-match shows a dedicated empty state.
  • Popular servers remain a separate discovery area (inside the add-server dialog, never mixed with active connections). Skills keep the installed/discoverable split with progress and error banners from Plan 2.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Sandbox setup (done)
docs.text:
• The setup card is a readiness flow: distribution name comes from state (fixing a stale hard-coded "Alpine Linux"), a Needs setup / Installing / Failed status badge, the distro's own storage-expectation copy, a session-persistence line, progress with cancel, and an error that is never the only content on screen.
  • After a failure the primary action becomes "Retry setup" instead of repeating the original invitation.
  • Skills already link to the sandbox setup flow via the Phase 1 prerequisite badge + button.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Sandbox workspace (done)
docs.text:
• Common workspace header (semantic heading() + Ready status badge) shared by Terminal, Files, and Packages.
  • Subtab selector: previously every tab was primary-colored, making the active tab invisible; now only the selected tab is primary + semibold, with Role.Tab and selected semantics.
  • Session chips get Role.Tab/selected semantics and a larger (8dp vertical) touch target.
  • Session selection stays above the terminal on all sizes (existing model); each pane keeps its own scroll container.

docs.title: Phase 5 — Accessibility, safety, and validation (done, with notes)
docs.text:
• Skill uninstall now requires explicit confirmation via SettingsConfirmDialog, matching file delete and package uninstall (which already confirmed). MCP server removal and service deletion keep their Plan 2 confirmations.
  • Stateful controls in the workspace carry accessible names/state: tab selectors and session chips expose Role.Tab + selected; file/package action icons have either a content description or are decorative next to labeled text.
  • Deferred / out of scope: a per-session close action (the session view model has no close operation — adding one changes behavior, not just UI), screenshot automation, and a full keyboard-navigation audit pass. These stay open as follow-ups.

docs.title: DORAI AI — UI Upgrade Plan 5: Services and Sponsors
Objective
docs.text: Turn the Services tab into a clear place to connect, manage, prioritise, and inspect AI services. Rework the sponsor area as a responsive expand/collapse grid where the DORAI AI profile is always the first card.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
• ServicesContent shows configured services in a reorderable list, an Add Service bottom sheet, and the Free tier card.
  • FreeSettings merges fallback settings, sponsorship calls to action, current/past sponsors, and partnership copy in one card.
  • SponsorList displays every remote sponsor immediately in a fixed-width FlowRow.
  • Sponsor data is fetched separately as current and past GitHub sponsors. The project README identifies the DORAI AI fork profile as habibbrox2; it should be the initial owner-profile data source until the final public profile copy, avatar, and destination URL are approved.

docs.title: Target experience
docs.text:
• A user can see which services are active, connected, unavailable, or need attention before opening a card.
  • Configured services remain reorderable, while their important details stay readable at a glance.
  • Adding a provider is a guided choice with provider identity, required credentials, supported capabilities, and any local-network requirement.
  • The Free tier and sponsor content are visually distinct from service configuration.
  • The sponsor section starts with the DORAI AI profile card. It stays visible in both collapsed and expanded states.
  • The sponsor grid shows a useful first set of cards, then reveals the remaining sponsors with a clear Show all / Collapse action only when more cards exist.

docs.title: Information architecture
docs.text:
Services
├── Service overview
├── Configured services
│   ├── Service status and selected model
│   └── Expanded configuration
├── Add service
├── Free tier and fallback
└── Support DORAI AI
    ├── DORAI AI profile (first)
    ├── Sponsor grid
    └── Show all / Collapse sponsors

docs.title: Target structure
docs.text:
ServicesContent
├── ServicesOverview
├── ConfiguredServicesList
│   └── ServiceCard
├── AddServiceSheet
├── FreeTierCard
└── SupportSection
    ├── OwnerProfileCard
    ├── SponsorGrid
    └── SponsorGridToggle

docs.title: Sponsor profile and ordering
docs.text:
Create a presentation model that can combine the static DORAI AI profile with remote sponsor entries without changing the sponsor API contract.

@Immutable
data class SupportProfile(
    val id: String,
    val name: String,
    val subtitle: String?,
    val avatarUrl: String?,
    val destinationUrl: String?,
    val isOwnerProfile: Boolean,
    val isCurrentSponsor: Boolean,
)
  1. Build the profile list in the view-model or a dedicated mapper: owner profile first, current sponsors next, then past sponsors not already listed.
  2. Give the owner profile a stable ID such as brox-kai-owner; do not treat it as a remote GitHub sponsor.
  3. Start its content from the repository identity (habibbrox2 / DORAI AI maintainer) and replace its public title, portrait, support link, and profile link with approved values before release.
  4. Use a local branded avatar fallback when a network avatar is unavailable. Show a neutral initial/avatar fallback if no approved profile image exists.
  5. Keep every destination optional in the model. A card with no approved link remains informational and must not appear tappable.

docs.title: Expand/collapse behaviour
docs.text:
Layout width Collapsed visible cards Expanded state Compact phone 2 All cards, one column Medium tablet 4 All cards, two columns Desktop / wide window 6 All cards, three columns
  • The owner profile is always index 0 and is never hidden by the collapsed limit.
  • Show the toggle only when the number of profiles exceeds the applicable collapsed limit.
  • The collapsed label reads Show all sponsors and includes the hidden count in its accessibility description. The expanded label reads Collapse sponsors.
  • Keep the section in the existing settings scroll container. For this short collection, use FlowRow or a simple responsive row layout instead of nesting a scrolling lazy grid inside the page.
  • Animate the grid height or content change with a short, reduced-motion-respecting transition. Preserve focus on the toggle after collapse.
  • Keep the current/past sponsor distinction in the data model. It may be shown as a subtle “Supporter” detail in the expanded view, but it must not move the owner card from first position.

docs.title: Visual direction
docs.text:
• Use Midnight Navy surfaces with restrained Cyan and Electric Blue accents from the DORAI AI theme.
  • Give the owner profile a modest featured treatment: avatar, DORAI AI name, maintainer subtitle, and one clear external-link action when a URL is approved.
  • Render sponsor cards with equal visual weight. Avoid oversized logos, multiple competing buttons, or dense text.
  • Keep connected/error service status text visible alongside the icon; color alone cannot carry status.
  • Keep cards, fields, and buttons aligned to the existing adaptive card styling so the tab feels part of Settings.

docs.title: State ownership
docs.text:
• Preserve SettingsUiState and SettingsActions for service configuration, ordering, connection checks, and provider mutations.
  • Continue fetching remote sponsors in SettingsViewModel; map the owner profile and remote entries to presentation items before the composable renders them.
  • Keep isSponsorGridExpanded as UI-only state at the Services/Support section boundary. It should reset when leaving the screen unless product requirements call for persistent preference storage.
  • Keep card click handling outside the item model: open only approved external destinations through the existing URI handler.
  • Do not let sponsor UI fetch network data or mutate service settings directly.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Service hierarchy
docs.text:
1. Add a compact Services overview that explains configured-service count and any service requiring attention.
  2. Improve each configured-service card header with provider name, selected model, connection status, and clear expand/reorder affordances.
  3. Keep API keys and advanced fields inside the existing expanded detail area.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Add-service flow
docs.text:
1. Group providers in the bottom sheet by common hosted providers, local/on-device, and OpenAI-compatible custom endpoints.
  2. Show a short setup requirement summary before a provider is added.
  3. Keep the existing action pipeline and validation; the sheet only changes presentation and guidance.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Sponsor profile and grid
docs.text:
1. Add the owner-profile mapper and approved content configuration.
  2. Replace SponsorList with SupportSection, OwnerProfileCard, SponsorGrid, and SponsorGridToggle.
  3. Deduplicate current and past sponsors as today, then prepend the owner profile.
  4. Apply the responsive collapsed limits and disclosure action.
  5. Keep the sponsorship and business-partnership calls to action below the grid with their links owned by configuration.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Polish and accessibility
docs.text:
1. Add accessible names for service status, drag handles, owner profile links, sponsor links, and the disclosure control.
  2. Ensure every card and toggle has a 48 dp minimum touch target and works with keyboard focus on desktop.
  3. Verify large-font wrapping, missing avatars, no network response, empty sponsors, and one-card sponsor lists.
  4. Respect reduced motion where platform settings expose it.

docs.title: Validation cases
docs.text:
• No configured services, one configured service, and multiple reordered services.
  • Connected, checking, invalid key, quota exhausted, and local-network-permission service statuses.
  • No remote sponsors: the DORAI AI profile card still renders first.
  • Sponsor counts at, below, and above each collapsed threshold.
  • Collapse after expansion returns focus to the toggle and never hides the owner profile.
  • Compact, medium, and desktop width screenshots with default and large font scales.
  • Avatar loading, avatar failure, no approved profile URL, and external-link interaction.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• Services can be configured and reordered without scrolling through sponsor content to find core controls.
  • The owner profile appears as the first card in the sponsor area for every state.
  • Sponsor lists larger than the viewport-friendly limit expand and collapse predictably; shorter lists have no redundant toggle.
  • The sponsor grid stays responsive, accessible, and free of nested-scroll problems.
  • Existing service actions, sponsor fetching, and Free tier fallback behaviour retain their current ownership and functionality.

docs.title: Risks and controls
docs.text:
• The existing feed is tied to the upstream sponsor account. Keep remote sponsor fetch failures non-blocking and preserve the static DORAI AI profile when the feed is unavailable.
  • Profile image, wording, and public destination must be approved before release. Use a branded fallback asset until those values are available.
  • A large remote sponsor list can make reflow expensive. Render only the collapsed subset until expanded and keep card content lightweight.
  • External links are user-visible destinations. Keep them in configuration and do not hardcode unverified personal URLs in the composable.

docs.title: Progress status
docs.text: All four phases are implemented, each compiled against the desktop target and committed separately.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Service hierarchy (done)
docs.text:
• Compact ServicesOverview card at the top of the Services tab: configured count plus a status badge (N needs attention / Checking connections / All connected); a dedicated empty state replaces the blank list when nothing is configured.
  • Configured-service card headers show provider name, selected model, and now a text connection-status badge instead of the color-only dot — covering every ConnectionStatus (Not checked, Checking, Connected, Invalid API key, Quota exhausted, Rate limited, Connection failed, Network blocked, Error).
  • API keys and advanced fields stay inside the existing expanded detail area; expand/reorder behavior untouched.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Add-service flow (done)
docs.text:
• The add-service sheet groups providers into Hosted providers, On-device, and Custom endpoints (headers hidden for empty groups), keeping first/last row corner rounding across groups.
  • Each row shows a setup requirement summary derived from Service metadata: runs on this device / custom endpoint / API key from \<portal> / key required / optional / none.
  • Action pipeline and validation unchanged — presentation and guidance only.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Sponsor profile and grid (done)
docs.text:
• SupportProfile presentation model and buildSupportProfiles mapper: owner profile first (stable id brox-kai-owner, repository identity habibbrox2, local branded logo avatar — no network dependency), then current sponsors, then past (deduplicated as before). The GitHub sponsors API contract is unchanged and fetching stays in SettingsViewModel.
  • SponsorList replaced by SupportSection + OwnerProfileCard + SponsorGrid: responsive collapse at 600/900dp shows 2/4/6 tiles, Show all sponsors / Collapse sponsors toggle with the hidden count in its accessibility description, short animateContentSize transition that keeps focus on the toggle. Lists at or below the limit render fully with no redundant toggle (acceptance criteria).
  • Expanded view keeps the current/past distinction with section labels; the owner card is never hidden by the limit.
  • Cards without a destination URL would render informational (no tap affordance); link actions carry accessible names; all support-area URLs are centralized in the SupportLinks configuration block (owner profile, sponsor base, become-sponsor, partnerships — the latter two keep their existing upstream destinations).
  • Sponsorship and partnership calls to action now sit below the grid.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Polish and accessibility (done, with notes)
docs.text:
• Accessible names: service status badges (Status: …), drag handles (existing reorder description), owner/sponsor links (action + destination in the description), disclosure control (hidden count).
  • Drag handle gains a 48dp minimum touch target around its 24dp glyph (minimumInteractiveComponentSize); cards and toggles are clickable/focusable through their existing Material components.
  • Validation performed by review: missing avatars fall back to the branded logo (owner) or a neutral initial (sponsors), an empty feed still renders the owner card first, one-card and threshold-crossing lists behave per the toggle rules above.
  • Deferred / out of scope: platform-specific reduced-motion detection (animateContentSize uses the default short duration), automated screenshot validation of every validation case, and persistent collapse-preference storage (state resets with the screen, per plan).

docs.title: DORAI AI — UI Upgrade Plan 6: Home Dashboard
Objective
docs.text: Create a calm starting screen for DORAI AI that gives users immediate access to Chat, Build, Design, and Tools, plus recent work and service readiness. The dashboard should shorten the path to a useful action without replacing the focused chat workspace.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
• The Home navigation route currently opens ChatScreen directly.
  • Desktop navigation has only Chat and Settings. On mobile, settings is reached from the chat UI.
  • DORAI Build opens as a transient surface from Chat on supported Android devices.
  • Recent conversations, provider selection, service status, build projects, and tools already have separate state holders or screens.

The dashboard is therefore a new presentation and navigation layer. It should compose existing capabilities rather than recreate their business logic.

docs.title: Target experience
docs.text:
• On launch, users see a clear next step: start a chat, create a build project, open Design, or manage tools.
  • Recent conversations and projects are visible without overwhelming the page.
  • A small readiness summary shows the selected AI service and any actionable setup issue.
  • The first screen remains fast, sparse, and useful whether the user has no history or many saved projects.
  • Selecting a card opens the existing destination with the appropriate context; it does not create a parallel feature flow.

docs.title: Information architecture
docs.text:
Home Dashboard
├── Welcome and service readiness
├── Primary actions
│   ├── Chat
│   ├── Build
│   ├── Design
│   └── Tools
├── Recent work
│   ├── Conversations
│   └── Build projects
├── Quick access
│   ├── Services
│   ├── Settings
│   └── Sandbox when available
└── Empty-state guidance

docs.title: Target structure
docs.text:
HomeDashboardScreen
├── DashboardHeader
│   ├── Brand greeting
│   └── ServiceReadinessPill
├── PrimaryActionGrid
│   ├── ChatActionCard
│   ├── BuildActionCard
│   ├── DesignActionCard
│   └── ToolsActionCard
├── RecentWorkSection
│   ├── RecentConversationList
│   └── RecentProjectList
├── QuickAccessRow
└── DashboardEmptyState

docs.title: Navigation model
docs.text:
1. Keep Chat as its own focused workspace. Introduce a separate Dashboard route instead of making the existing Home route carry two incompatible responsibilities.
  2. Make Dashboard the launch destination after the feature is complete; retain Chat as a first-class primary destination.
  3. Add navigation destinations through a typed route and one central navigation coordinator. Dashboard cards dispatch navigation events rather than calling feature view models.
  4. Route Build only where it is currently supported. Unsupported platforms show a disabled, explanatory card or omit Build according to the product capability policy.
  5. Treat Design as a destination contract. Until a dedicated design workspace exists, its action may open the existing interactive creation flow with a Design-focused prompt or show an honest “coming soon” state; it must not claim a separate editor exists.
  6. Open Tools through Settings with the Tools tab selected, and Services through Settings with the Services tab selected. The selected-tab action remains owned by SettingsViewModel.

docs.title: Primary actions
docs.text:
• Show Chat first, then Build, Design, and Tools in a stable order.
  • Each card has one title, a short purpose statement, a recognisable icon, and optional readiness state.
  • Use Cyan or Electric Blue only for the primary action and current focus. Keep other cards Midnight Navy with clear outlines and text contrast.
  • If setup is needed, keep the main card actionable and surface the requirement in a small supporting label.

docs.title: Recent work
docs.text:
• Show up to four recent conversations and four recent build projects on wide layouts; show two of each on compact layouts.
  • Each conversation row includes title, last activity, selected service/model when available, and a compact resume affordance.
  • Each project row includes project name, last activity, and build or environment status when known.
  • Place View all only when more saved items exist. It opens the existing history or project hub rather than loading an unbounded list into the dashboard.
  • Do not show sensitive prompt previews by default. Use a generic title or the existing conversation title.

docs.title: Readiness and empty states
docs.text:
• If a usable service is configured, show its name and selected model in a compact readiness pill.
  • If no service is configured, replace the pill with a clear Set up a service action that opens Services.
  • With no saved work, retain the primary action grid and show a short starter suggestion beneath it.
  • If Build, Sandbox, or Tools are unavailable, use capability state supplied by the platform/view model; do not infer availability in a composable.

docs.title: Responsive layout
docs.text:
Width Primary actions Recent work Navigation Compact Two-column cards, stacked sections Two rows per collection Bottom/top compact navigation Medium Two-column cards with balanced spacing Two-column recent sections Compact rail or top navigation Expanded Four action cards in one row Conversations and projects side by side Persistent sidebar or top navigation
  • Keep the dashboard as one vertically scrolling surface with section spacing rather than nested scrolling lists.
  • Let primary action cards grow with text scale; never truncate the primary action label.
  • Maintain an obvious keyboard focus order: header, primary actions, recent work, then quick access.

docs.title: State ownership
docs.text:
• Create DashboardUiState as a read-only aggregation of existing feature summaries: selected service, service readiness, recent conversation summaries, recent project summaries, and capability flags.
  • Keep full chat history in ChatViewModel, full project lifecycle in KaiBuildViewModel, and settings mutations in SettingsViewModel.
  • A dashboard coordinator/repository maps small, display-safe summaries from those sources. It contains no prompt content, credentials, terminal output, or mutable service configuration.
  • Keep UI-only state local: temporary loading shimmer visibility, a dismissed welcome hint, and small-screen section expansion if needed.
  • Dashboard clicks emit navigation and resume events through interfaces; cards do not access data stores or view models directly.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Foundation and routes
docs.text:
1. Add a typed Dashboard route and central navigation events for Chat, Build, Settings tabs, history, and projects.
  2. Define DashboardUiState and display-safe recent-work summary models.
  3. Add capability flags for Build, Sandbox, and Design destinations.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Dashboard shell
docs.text:
1. Build the header, service-readiness pill, primary action cards, and empty state using DORAI AI colors and typography.
  2. Add responsive spacing and grid policy for compact, medium, and expanded layouts.
  3. Connect Chat and Settings cards first, then gate platform-specific destinations from capability state.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Recent work
docs.text:
1. Map conversation and project data to display-safe dashboard summaries.
  2. Add resume actions and View all routes to existing history and project-hub experiences.
  3. Ensure opening a recent item preserves the selected conversation or project instead of creating a duplicate session.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Design and tools pathways
docs.text:
1. Define the Design destination contract and use the existing interactive flow only when it satisfies that contract.
  2. Add Tools, Services, and Sandbox quick-access actions with selected settings tabs.
  3. Make unavailable capabilities clear without presenting broken navigation.

docs.title: Phase 5 — Accessibility and validation
docs.text:
1. Give action cards, readiness status, recent-item actions, and unavailable states descriptive semantics.
  2. Verify 48 dp targets, keyboard navigation, focus restoration after returning from a destination, and large-font layouts.
  3. Add screenshot cases for first launch, configured service, no service, populated history, populated projects, loading summaries, and unavailable Build/Design states.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• The first screen lets a new user reach Chat, service setup, and available creation tools in one interaction.
  • Returning users can resume recent conversations and projects without navigating through unrelated settings.
  • Dashboard summaries do not duplicate provider, chat, or build business logic.
  • Unsupported capabilities are represented truthfully and never lead to a dead end.
  • Compact and desktop layouts preserve clear hierarchy, accessibility, and low visual clutter.

docs.title: Progress status
docs.text:
• [x] Phase 1 — Foundation and routes (Dashboard route + Build route, DashboardUiState + mapper, capability flags)
  • [x] Phase 2 — Dashboard shell (header, readiness card, primary action grid responsive, Chat/Settings/Build gating)
  • [x] Phase 3 — Recent work (conversations and projects, resume, View all)
  • [x] Phase 4 — Design and tools pathways (Design prefill contract, Tools/Services via Settings tabs, unavailable capabilities honest)
  • [x] Phase 5 — Accessibility and validation (basic semantics on cards; screenshot cases to be validated on device)

docs.title: Risks and controls
docs.text:
• Aggregating feature state can create startup delay. Render the action grid immediately and independently load recent-work summaries.
  • Recent conversations may expose private content. Display only existing safe titles and metadata, never prompt excerpts by default.
  • Design does not yet have a dedicated workspace. Keep the Design entry behind an explicit destination contract until the workflow exists.
  • Route changes can break back-stack behavior. Add navigation tests for launch, returning from Chat, Settings, Build, and recent-item resume actions.

docs.title: DORAI AI — Premium AI Agent Workspace UI (2027 Direction)
docs.text: Document type: Product/UI migration plan Status: Core 2027 UI foundation is present in main; responsive, accessibility, reduced-motion, and visual-regression refinements are in progress. Platforms: Android, Desktop, Web via Kotlin Multiplatform + Compose

docs.title: 1. Product vision
docs.text:
DORAI AI should feel like a premium AI Agent Workspace: chat-first, calm, responsive, and capable of presenting interactive work products inline. The interface combines a compact Agent HUD, multimodal composer, safe generative micro-canvases, visible execution activity, and a dockable coding/terminal workspace.

The design borrows interaction patterns from modern AI products without copying their implementation. The app remains Compose Multiplatform and preserves its existing runtime and platform boundaries.

docs.title: 2. Non-negotiable product decisions
docs.text:
• Brand: “DORAI AI” remains the product name.
  • Primary destination: Chat remains the home experience.
  • Navigation: history/sidebar and Settings remain accessible without a crowded tab strip in the header.
  • Dashboard: preserve its existing route/entry point; do not remove features as part of the visual refresh.
  • Interactive UI: remains part of the same chat and uses the existing kai-ui renderer.
  • Code editor: keep the unified editor/workspace flow; mobile may use a full-screen route, expanded desktop may use a split panel.
  • Runtime integrity: provider calls, persistence, MCP, sandbox execution, and tool permissions remain outside composables.
  • Capability honesty: no fake mic, camera, attachment, terminal, latency, or token-usage controls.
  • Privacy: show observable agent activity, not hidden chain-of-thought.

docs.title: 3. Current-state baseline
docs.text:
Previously inspected repository documentation describes:

  • An adaptive ChatShell with a conversation rail and optional side panel on expanded windows.
  • A compact header with history/new-chat/workspace/speech/settings controls.
  • A fixed bottom QuestionInput with attachment handling, skill autocomplete, service selection, and send/stop behavior.
  • Assistant response actions such as copy, retry, share, and speech.
  • A JSON-based kai-ui renderer for interactive layouts in chat.
  • A unified editor workspace with file tree, editable code view, and terminal tab.
  • Settings categories covering General, Agent, Services, Tools, Integrations, Sandbox, Data, and Account.

This is a baseline from existing docs, not a guarantee that every item remains unchanged in the current branch. Re-audit source and tests before implementation.

docs.title: 4.1 Design language
docs.text:
• Deep Obsidian/OLED foundation with layered charcoal surfaces.
  • Restrained cyan for primary actions and active controls.
  • Electric violet for agent/tool activity, used sparingly.
  • Fine borders and subtle depth; avoid excessive blur and neon.
  • Typography optimized for readability and platform availability.
  • JetBrains Mono or another bundled monospace font for terminal/editor content after licensing and packaging checks.
  • Motion should be responsive, short, and optional under reduced-motion settings.

docs.title: 4.2 Initial tokens
docs.text:
Token Initial value color.background #090A0F color.surface rgba(255,255,255,0.04) color.surfaceElevated #171A23 color.borderSubtle rgba(255,255,255,0.08) color.accentPrimary #00D7E8 color.accentAgent #8A63F6 color.terminalBackground #0B0D11 shape.control 12–16dp shape.card 18–24dp

These are starting tokens. Validate contrast and theme semantics before locking them. Do not use raw values directly in feature composables.

docs.title: Screen 1 — Home / empty chat
docs.text:
• Centered DORAI AI identity/orb with a subtle ambient animation.
  • Clear welcome headline and concise helper text.
  • Horizontal quick-action chips instead of oversized fixed cards.
  • Chips are contextual and state-aware: Resume RPG, Ask a question, Run sandbox check, Daily reminders.
  • The composer remains visible and reachable.
  • Animation supports static/reduced-motion rendering.

docs.title: Screen 2 — Conversation
docs.text:
• Compact user bubbles and aligned assistant response column.
  • Avoid large nested message containers and card-within-card styling.
  • Preserve markdown, code, image, table, and attachment rendering.
  • Add a compact response action bar: Copy, Retry/Regenerate, Share, Speak, and feedback where implemented.
  • Keep streaming/cancel status separate from final answer content.
  • Scrolling must not jump while the user is reading earlier messages.

docs.title: Screen 3 — Generative micro-canvas
docs.text:
Use kai-ui to render context-specific interactive work products.

RPG/game widget - Compact stats and animated HP/progress indicators. - Responsive artwork and readable narrative. - Action buttons use typed callbacks. - State remains owned by the conversation or game feature, not transient composable state.

Recipe/workflow widget - Scrollable checklist with explicit completion state. - Clear step hierarchy and ingredient quantities. - Accessible alternative to visual progress.

Data widget - Schema-validated tables/charts and filter controls. - Explicit units and labels. - Text/table fallback and bounded data sizes.

docs.title: Screen 4 — Agent activity
docs.text:
• Collapsed activity summary above/near the assistant response.
  • Expanded chronological list of actual MCP/native/sandbox operations.
  • Show tool name, concise sanitized summary, status, duration if measured, and bounded result preview.
  • Support waiting-for-approval, running, success, failure, and cancellation.
  • Never show private chain-of-thought or raw hidden reasoning.
  • Never expose secrets, credentials, or unrestricted command output.

docs.title: Screen 5 — Universal Action Bar
docs.text:
• Plus menu for supported camera/gallery/file actions.
  • Multiline text field with draft preservation.
  • Slash command picker for registered skills/MCP tools.
  • Voice input only where a working speech-to-text path exists.
  • Clear Send and Stop states.
  • Attachment tray with preview and remove controls.
  • Respect IME/keyboard insets, focus order, and desktop shortcuts.

docs.title: Screen 6 — Terminal and code workspace
docs.text:
• Compact devices: docked bottom sheet or full-screen workspace.
  • Expanded desktop: resizable split pane beside chat.
  • Terminal surface: #0B0D11, readable monospace, selection/copy, syntax highlighting where available.
  • Tool-to-terminal handoff must be explicit and limited to approved/safe commands.
  • Existing sandbox process, filesystem, and permission boundaries remain authoritative.
  • Do not imply identical shell support on Android, Desktop, and Web.

docs.title: Screen 7 — Settings and services
docs.text:
• Compact horizontal category strip with scroll-to-selected behavior.
  • Expanded rail/sidebar navigation.
  • Slim service cards with provider/model, status, and diagnostics.
  • Latency and token counts only when the runtime provides real measurements.
  • Consistent toggles, labels, helper text, and error states.
  • Avoid duplicate or overflowing navigation pills.

docs.title: 6. Architecture mapping
docs.text:
The app is Compose Multiplatform. Use these as logical boundaries and adapt to the existing source tree:

UI responsibility Suggested Compose boundary Dynamic header AgentHud, AgentStatusIndicator Agent execution trace AgentActivityDisclosure Interactive response blocks Existing KaiUiRenderer and typed node model Composer Existing QuestionInput evolved into UniversalComposer Attachments/slash actions Composer subcomponents/sheets Terminal/editor Existing workspace/editor and sandbox UI Glass surfaces Shared theme/component primitives Runtime state Existing ViewModel, state, actions, and runtime event contracts

Avoid creating parallel React-style src/components or a second AgentRuntime provider. Extend the existing Kotlin architecture.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Foundation and theming
docs.text:
Deliverables - Semantic color, surface, border, radius, spacing, and typography tokens. - OLED, dark, and light theme validation. - Shared glass surface, status pill, icon button, and quick chip components. - Reduced-motion and blur fallback behavior. - Screenshot fixtures and contrast checks.

Exit criteria - No hard-coded palette drift in migrated components. - Theme tests and baseline screenshots pass. - Large text and accessibility contrast are acceptable.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Core shell and action bar
docs.text:
Deliverables - Compact Agent HUD replacing the vertical AI Agent badge. - Adaptive header actions and overflow behavior. - Empty-state quick chips and ambient orb. - Capability-aware universal composer. - Draft/attachment persistence through sheet and layout transitions.

Exit criteria - No header or tab overflow on compact screens. - Keyboard does not cover composer or latest message. - Every visible action is connected to a real capability.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Generative UI and activity trace
docs.text:
Deliverables - Versioned/validated kai-ui schema evolution with backward compatibility. - Component registry improvements where justified by current renderer. - RPG, recipe, and data micro-canvas patterns. - Runtime-backed activity trace with safe summaries. - Consistent response action bar.

Exit criteria - Old saved kai-ui messages still render. - Invalid/untrusted model output cannot execute arbitrary code or privileged actions. - Activity events reflect real runtime operations and redact secrets.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Terminal and settings polish
docs.text:
Deliverables - Dockable terminal/workspace presentation. - Explicit safe tool-to-terminal handoff. - Compact settings category strip and expanded rail. - Service status cards using real runtime diagnostics. - Motion and interaction polish.

Exit criteria - Terminal process ownership and sandbox permissions are unchanged. - Settings navigation works at compact and expanded widths. - Unsupported platform capabilities are clearly hidden or disabled with explanation.

docs.title: Phase 5 — Regression and release readiness
docs.text:
Deliverables - Unit, serialization, screenshot, and UI regression tests. - Android/Desktop/Web builds for supported targets. - Accessibility and performance checks. - Documentation updates and reviewable pull request.

Exit criteria - Existing provider, chat, MCP, sandbox, interactive UI, and editor workflows remain functional. - No critical crash, layout overflow, or secret exposure. - All required CI checks pass.

docs.title: 8. Testing matrix
docs.text: Area Required scenarios Header Idle, streaming, tool-running, waiting, error; compact and expanded Composer Empty, draft, multiline, attachments, slash menu, send, stop, keyboard Timeline Long response, code, table, image, streaming, manual scroll, retry Activity Concurrent tools, approval, success, failure, cancellation, redaction kai-ui Old schema, new schema, invalid JSON, oversized tree, historical read-only Workspace Open/close dock, resize split, terminal unavailable, process cancellation Settings All categories, selected-tab visibility, large font, narrow width Themes Light, dark, OLED, contrast, reduced motion Platforms Android, Desktop, Web targets currently supported by the repository

docs.title: 9. Risks and mitigations
docs.text:
• Large chat screen refactor: extract one boundary at a time and preserve behavior with screenshot tests.
  • Compose platform differences: keep platform APIs behind existing source-set abstractions.
  • Blur/rendering cost: use blur sparingly and retain opaque/translucent fallbacks.
  • Agent activity privacy: sanitize at the runtime boundary, not only in UI.
  • Generative UI attack surface: strict schema allowlist, size limits, typed actions, and no dynamic code execution.
  • Runtime regressions: no provider, persistence, MCP, or sandbox business logic migration during visual-only changes.
  • False capability claims: hide controls when the platform/runtime does not provide the feature.

docs.title: 10. Rollback strategy
docs.text:
• Keep each phase independently reviewable.
  • Avoid changing persisted data formats unless backward-compatible defaults and migration tests exist.
  • Gate new UI affordances behind existing settings or a feature flag where appropriate.
  • Retain the previous component path until screenshot and interaction parity is demonstrated.
  • Revert presentation changes without reverting provider/runtime fixes.

docs.title: 11. Definition of done
docs.text: A phase is complete only when its implementation, tests, screenshots, and documentation are reviewed. A visual mockup or successful compile alone is not sufficient. No phase is considered released until its required CI checks pass and the owner explicitly approves the release path.

docs.title: Kotlin / TypeScript Communication Contrac
docs.text: Initial protocol: brox-kai-hybrid 1.0 Status: Schema foundation only; no transport implementation.

docs.title: Envelope types
docs.text:
Envelope Required identity Purpose Request requestId Ask Kotlin-owned host for a defined operation Response requestId Return result or structured error Event eventId, sessionId, sequence Publish ordered runtime state/activity

Schemas are in hybrid/contracts/schemas/.

docs.title: Normative requirements for future implementations
docs.text:
• Validate JSON against the matching schema before dispatch.
  • Reject unsupported major versions and unknown operation types.
  • Match responses to outstanding request IDs; reject unsolicited or stale responses.
  • Bound message bytes, nesting, collection sizes, and string lengths.
  • Enforce timeouts, cancellation, concurrency limits, and backpressure.
  • Authenticate the transport endpoint/session where applicable.
  • Authorize every operation at the Kotlin capability layer; schema validation is not authorization.
  • Redact secrets from logs and error messages.
  • Do not pass arbitrary Kotlin reflection names, class names, shell commands, or filesystem paths as generic operations.

A transport must not be implemented until its lifecycle and threat model are documented for each target.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text: Establish a safe, versioned foundation for Kotlin and TypeScript to coexist without coupling their build systems or transferring privileged ownership to the TypeScript side.

docs.title: 2. Runtime topology
docs.text:
Kotlin is the application and capability authority. TypeScript is an independently built frontend/integration platform. A bridge is a later implementation decision and is not part of this foundation.

Potential transports must be selected per deployment target only after evaluating lifecycle, origin isolation, serialization, cancellation, and threat model. Do not assume that Android WebView, desktop browser, and hosted web require the same transport.

docs.title: 3. Contract model
docs.text:
The initial protocol uses JSON envelopes:

  • Request: request ID, message type, protocol version, operation type, payload.
  • Response: matching request ID, success state, result or bounded error.
  • Event: event ID, session ID, monotonic sequence, event type, payload.

Schemas live in hybrid/contracts/schemas/. The protocol version is recorded in hybrid/contracts/protocol-version.json.

docs.title: 4. Capability security
docs.text:
• Kotlin validates every incoming message and independently checks authorization.
  • TypeScript receives only explicitly granted capabilities.
  • Never expose arbitrary shell commands, unrestricted filesystem paths, secrets, or raw platform objects through a generic bridge.
  • User confirmation is required for destructive or sensitive actions.
  • Apply request size, payload depth, string length, timeout, cancellation, and rate limits in runtime code.
  • Use origin/session binding and replay protection where the selected transport requires them.
  • Logs must redact secrets and bound payload output.

docs.title: 5. Reliability
docs.text:
• Correlate requests and responses with unique request IDs.
  • Define timeout and cancellation semantics before transport implementation.
  • Events use a per-session monotonic sequence; consumers detect gaps and duplicates.
  • Errors use stable machine-readable codes and bounded user-safe messages.
  • Major protocol incompatibility fails closed.
  • Optional fields may be added compatibly; semantic changes require a versioning decision.

docs.title: 6. Existing Dynamic UI
docs.text: The current kai-ui JSON format remains a constrained Compose presentation protocol. It is not a JavaScript execution mechanism and should not be silently replaced by a TypeScript renderer. Any future browser renderer must preserve allowlisted node/action semantics and Kotlin-owned privileged operations.

docs.title: 7. Implementation sequence
docs.text:
1. Approve and stabilize shared schemas.
  2. Add Kotlin and TypeScript contract validation with shared fixtures.
  3. Select a transport per platform and document its threat model.
  4. Implement a narrow capability registry and authorization tests.
  5. Add lifecycle, cancellation, timeout, and observability tests.
  6. Integrate one low-risk feature end-to-end before expanding capabilities.

docs.title: Kotlin Platform Architecture
docs.text:
Kotlin Multiplatform remains the primary application platform.

  • Compose Multiplatform owns the current shared UI.
  • Kotlin owns agent orchestration, providers, tools, storage, and platform integrations.
  • Android, iOS, Desktop, and the existing Kotlin/Wasm target remain on their current Gradle configuration.
  • New TypeScript tooling must not require changes to Kotlin source sets or Gradle modules in this foundation phase.

The existing Kotlin/Wasm target compiles Kotlin for WebAssembly/browser deployment. It is not a TypeScript project and must not be conflated with the new TypeScript workspace.

Future Kotlin bridge adapters must validate shared protocol envelopes and authorize each operation independently of schema validation.

docs.title: DORAI AI System Architecture
docs.text: Status: Foundation architecture Scope: Kotlin-first hybrid platform

docs.title: Architectural direction
docs.text:
DORAI AI remains a Kotlin Multiplatform application with Compose Multiplatform as its native/shared UI foundation. TypeScript is introduced as an independent workspace for future web-facing, extension, SDK, and integration capabilities. It is not a replacement for the existing Kotlin application.

Android / Desktop / iOS / Web
            |
     Kotlin Multiplatform
  UI · Agent · Providers · Tools
            |
    Explicit capability boundary
            |
    Versioned JSON contracts
            |
     TypeScript workspace
 Web modules · SDK · Integrations

This diagram describes intended ownership and contracts, not a currently implemented runtime bridge.

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text: Area Primary owner Application lifecycle and native UI Kotlin / Compose Agent orchestration and provider adapters Kotlin Tool execution, shell, filesystem, sandbox Kotlin Credentials and permission decisions Kotlin Existing Kotlin/Wasm target Kotlin toolchain Future browser-facing modules and SDKs TypeScript Cross-language message format Shared JSON Schema

docs.title: Build isolation
docs.text:
• Gradle remains the authoritative Kotlin build.
  • pnpm manages only the TypeScript workspace.
  • Node.js is a development/build toolchain, not an Android runtime dependency.
  • TypeScript build/test failure must not become a dependency of Android/Desktop Gradle tasks.
  • Existing Kotlin/Wasm compilation remains independent and unchanged.

docs.title: Security boundary
docs.text: TypeScript code is not trusted merely because it is bundled with the application. It must not receive unrestricted access to filesystem, shell, credentials, network secrets, or platform APIs. Any future bridge must expose narrow capabilities through Kotlin-owned validation, authorization, user approval, and audit logging.

docs.title: Non-goals of this foundation
docs.text:
• No migration of existing Kotlin features.
  • No React or other UI framework selection.
  • No plugin loader or arbitrary code execution.
  • No WebView bridge or IPC implementation.
  • No change to the current app runtime.

docs.title: Technology Boundaries
docs.text: Concern Kotlin TypeScript App lifecycle Authoritative Not authoritative Native/shared Compose UI Authoritative Not a replacement Agent orchestration Authoritative Requests only through approved APIs Provider credentials Owns secure storage/use Never receives raw secrets Shell/filesystem/sandbox Owns execution and permissions No unrestricted access Browser UI/integrations Host capability provider Future implementation Cross-language contracts Validates/consumes Validates/consumes Existing Kotlin/Wasm Owns target/build Separate workspace

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. Do not duplicate business logic across languages without a documented reason.
  2. Keep transport DTOs separate from domain models.
  3. Never treat TypeScript validation as a security boundary.
  4. Do not execute model-generated or remotely supplied code in privileged contexts.
  5. Keep Gradle and pnpm dependency graphs independent.
  6. Any future exception requires an Architecture Decision Record.

docs.title: Role
docs.text: The TypeScript workspace is a separate platform foundation for future browser-facing modules, extension integrations, plugin SDKs, and web tooling. It does not replace Compose or existing Kotlin features.

docs.title: Current toolchain
docs.text:
• pnpm workspace
  • TypeScript strict compiler configuration
  • Vite build/dev foundation
  • Vitest test foundation
  • Prettier formatting

No UI framework, production bundler entry point, runtime bridge, or plugin API is selected in this phase.

docs.title: Source organization
docs.text:
Future code should be introduced as explicit packages under the workspace. Each package must declare its runtime target, public API, dependencies, test strategy, and security boundary.

Do not place secrets or privileged operations in browser code. Avoid dynamic code evaluation and unsafe HTML injection. Validate all data crossing a trust boundary.

docs.title: Dependency policy
docs.text: Add production dependencies only when an approved feature requires them. Keep build/test tools in development dependencies. Pin the package manager and commit the lockfile. Review licenses, maintenance, supply-chain posture, and bundle/runtime impact before adding dependencies.

docs.title: ADR-001: Kotlin-first hybrid language strategy
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted for foundation
  • Date: 2026-11-03
  • Decision owners: DORAI AI maintainers

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The application is already built on Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform, with Android, iOS, Desktop, and Kotlin/Wasm targets. Future web and integration work may benefit from TypeScript, but replacing the existing UI/runtime or coupling the Gradle build to Node would add migration and operational risk.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Keep Kotlin as the primary application, agent, provider, tool, storage, and privileged capability platform.
  2. Add an independent pnpm-managed TypeScript workspace for future web-facing modules and SDKs.
  3. Define cross-language communication using versioned, language-neutral JSON Schema.
  4. Keep the current Kotlin/Wasm target independent from the TypeScript workspace.
  5. Do not add a runtime bridge or migrate existing features in this foundation phase.
  6. Keep TypeScript tooling outside Gradle task dependencies.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Kotlin and TypeScript can evolve independently.
  • Shared contracts become explicit and reviewable.
  • A future bridge requires a separate transport/security design and implementation.
  • Initial TypeScript application sources remain empty by design.
  • Additional frameworks and runtime dependencies require feature-level approval.

docs.title: Rejected alternatives
docs.text:
• Replace Compose with React: rejected because it would be a broad UI migration and duplicate existing platform work.
  • Execute arbitrary TypeScript inside the agent process: rejected due to security and lifecycle risks.
  • Reuse Kotlin/Wasm as if it were TypeScript: rejected because the language/toolchain and module ownership differ.

docs.title: Canonical product identity
docs.text:
• Product: DORAI AI
  • Category: Hybrid AI Assistant & Agent Platform
  • Android/iOS identifier: com.dorai.ai
  • Primary mark: dorai/symbol.svg

docs.title: Visual direction
docs.text:
• Primary background: Deep Navy #0B2B5B
  • Primary accent: Tech Cyan #00D1E8
  • Secondary accent: Blue #168BDB
  • Foreground: White #F4FAFF

Use the symbol consistently across app launchers, website favicon, desktop packages, and documentation. Do not recreate the old BK monogram or use legacy Kai wordmarks.

docs.title: Naming rules
docs.text:
• User-facing product name: DORAI AI
  • Short product reference: DORAI
  • Android/iOS bundle identity: com.dorai.ai
  • Release artifact prefix: DORAI-AI
  • Internal package namespace: com.dorai.ai

Keep upstream Kai 9000 references only where needed for attribution, license notices, or documented legacy infrastructure. Those references must never be presented as the current product identity.

docs.title: Canonical application identity
docs.text:
• Product name: DORAI AI
  • Android application ID: com.dorai.ai
  • Android application namespace: com.dorai.ai
  • Shared Kotlin namespace: com.dorai.ai.shared
  • iOS bundle ID: com.dorai.ai
  • iOS shared framework bundle ID: com.dorai.ai.composeapp
  • Gradle root project: dorai
  • SQLDelight database class: DoraIDatabase
  • Local SQL database file: dorai.db
  • Desktop distribution name: DORAI
  • Flatpak app ID: com.dorai.ai

docs.title: New-app installation model
docs.text: DORAI is a separate application, not an in-place rename of the legacy Kai installation. Android and iOS use new bundle/application identifiers. The old app can remain installed independently. No silent transfer of private app data is attempted. If user data import is added later, it must be an explicit, user-initiated, validated export/import flow.

docs.title: Updater safety
docs.text: The DORAI updater accepts only releases carrying DORAI-prefixed artifacts and a manifest whose package name is com.dorai.ai. Legacy releases without a DORAI APK are ignored. The stale pre-migration root update.json was removed because its checksum and signer fingerprint described a different application artifact. The first signed DORAI release must generate and publish a fresh manifest from the built APK; never reuse legacy APK checksums or signing fingerprints.

docs.title: External dependencies that require separate provisioning
docs.text:
The GitHub repository has been renamed to habibbrox2/DoraiAi; the local working folder remains G:\Web\broxkai2.0 until a separate local rename.

New Google Play and App Store listings must be registered for com.dorai.ai; legacy Kai store URLs are upstream references only. WinGet publishing is disabled until a DORAI package ID is registered. The legacy kai-bin AUR package and auto-publisher were removed; create a new dorai-bin package only after the first DORAI release provides a verifiable checksum. Do not publish DORAI installers under legacy package-manager identifiers.

The legacy service endpoint api.kai9000.com and website hostname kai9000.com are external infrastructure references. They must not be replaced with guessed DORAI domains or endpoints. Before retiring them, provision and verify DORAI-owned DNS, TLS, API routing, website hosting, and release hosting, then update the app and website configuration together.

Upstream attribution, copyright notices, and license references must remain intact. They identify the original upstream project and are not DORAI product identity.

docs.title: Release gate
docs.text: Do not publish a DORAI release until: - Android APK package name is verified as com.dorai.ai. - Release signing credentials and signer fingerprint are provisioned for the new app. - The generated update manifest matches the APK package, version, version code, asset name, SHA-256, and signer certificate. - Android, Desktop and iOS builds pass their applicable checks. Web/Wasm remains excluded from distribution until its compatibility backlog is resolved. - Website and DNS ownership for any new DORAI domain is verified before changing production endpoints.

docs.title: GitHub release-history and first-release gate
docs.text:
The renamed GitHub repository still retains legacy Kai release history. The latest published release is Brox Kai v2.1.3; legacy tags v2.1.4 and v2.1.5 also already exist. No DORAI release has been published. Do not direct users to the Releases page as a DORAI download source until a DORAI release exists; the current public copy explicitly marks the first release as pending.

The current source metadata still says appVersion = 2.1.4 and android-versionCode = 216. The v2.1.4 tag is already occupied by a legacy release, so it cannot be reused for DORAI. Before release, select a new unused semantic version and matching version code, then update gradle/libs.versions.toml. The release workflow now rejects a tag that does not match appVersion, and it requires the tag commit to already be merged into main before it can publish update.json there.

Google Play publishing is disabled unless the repository variable DORAI_PLAY_STORE_ENABLED=true is deliberately configured after the DORAI listing and credentials are ready. GitHub Pages deployment is manual-only and requires DORAI_SITE_DOMAIN to match site/CNAME, plus DORAI_WEB_WASM_ENABLED=true after Web/Wasm support is release-ready. No release, merge, push, or deployment is authorized by this migration work.

docs.title: DORAI AI Brand Assets
docs.text:
• symbol.svg — primary DORAI AI application symbol.
  • App icons are generated from the same navy/cyan mark and distributed in platform asset directories.
  • Keep wordmarks, favicons, launcher icons, and metadata aligned with the canonical identity in ../brand-name-usage.md.

docs.title: DORAI AI Theme Contract
docs.text: This document is the source-of-truth contract for the shared Compose Multiplatform color schemes.

docs.title: Theme modes
docs.text: Mode Background Surface Intent System Platform-selected Platform-selected Follow OS appearance Light #FFFFFF #F8FAFC Light neutral surfaces Dark #121212 Material dark neutral Standard dark appearance Midnight #050810 #0B1026 Brand navy workspace with cyan accents OLED Black #000000 #000000 True black base surfaces for OLED/AMOLED displays

docs.title: Brand palette
docs.text:
• Brand navy: #0B1026
  • Deep navy: #050810
  • Charcoal: #151B2B
  • Cyan accent: #22D3EE
  • Elevated navy surface: #0A0F1C
  • Raised navy surface: #111827

docs.title: Runtime mapping
docs.text:
App.kt maps persisted ThemeMode values to exactly one shared scheme:

  • ThemeMode.System → system-selected scheme
  • ThemeMode.Light → LightColorScheme
  • ThemeMode.Dark → DarkColorScheme
  • ThemeMode.Midnight → MidnightColorScheme
  • ThemeMode.OledBlack → OledColorScheme

Do not approximate OLED mode by changing only the background. The background, base surface, and lowest surface containers must remain #000000; elevated cards may use a distinct raised surface so hierarchy remains visible.

Midnight is not OLED. Its background must remain deep navy and its primary content surface must use brand navy. Do not classify it as OLED when selecting card treatments or other surface behavior.

docs.title: Implementation rules
docs.text:
1. Prefer shared tokens from Theme.kt over local duplicate color literals.
  2. Keep semantic tokens distinct from component-specific tokens. A component token should reference a semantic token when the visual intent is identical.
  3. Avoid using the OLED black token as ordinary dark-theme text unless the foreground sits on a sufficiently bright accent surface.
  4. Keep text, focus indicators, borders, and selected states distinguishable on both Midnight and OLED backgrounds.
  5. Any change to a theme mode must update the runtime mapping, color assertions, and screenshot coverage together.

docs.title: Verification matrix
docs.text:
• Unit assertions: OLED zero-black base surfaces; Midnight navy surfaces; standard Dark not misclassified as OLED.
  • Screenshot coverage: Chat and Settings on phone and tablet for Light, Dark, Midnight, and OLED.
  • Accessibility review: selected navigation semantics, keyboard focus visibility, and text/border contrast on all dark schemes.

docs.title: Visual Regression Matrix
docs.text: This matrix defines the required visual regression coverage for DORAI AI. Paparazzi screenshot tests are the baseline for deterministic Compose rendering; manual/runtime accessibility checks remain separate verification items.

docs.title: Theme and surface coverage
docs.text:
Surface Light Dark Midnight OLED Black Chat with messages Yes Yes Yes Yes Chat empty state Yes Existing baseline — — Chat dynamic UI Yes — — — Chat with Sandbox open — Yes — — Settings Agent — Yes Yes Yes Settings Free — Yes — — Settings Tools Yes — — —

System mode follows the host platform appearance and is verified through runtime/manual checks rather than a deterministic screenshot fixture.

docs.title: Device-size coverage
docs.text: Target Existing coverage Required review Phone portrait ScreenshotTest Chat, Settings, long localized labels Tablet TabletStoreScreenshotTest Chat and Settings in Light/Dark/Midnight/OLED Desktop compact (840–900 dp) Runtime/UI test required Conversation rail and Sandbox width constraints Desktop medium (1024 dp) Runtime/UI test required Main chat minimum width and composer Desktop wide (1280 dp+) Runtime/UI test required Rail, chat, and side panel coexistence

docs.title: Accessibility and localization review
docs.text:
• Settings desktop navigation exposes Role.Tab and selected state.
  • Settings mobile selector exposes Role.Tab, selected state, keyboard focus, and left/right arrow navigation.
  • Keyboard Tab and Shift+Tab retain normal focus traversal.
  • Review default font scale plus 1.3x, 1.5x, and 2.0x on phone/tablet.
  • Review English and Bengali labels; add German/French long-string fixtures when those locales are introduced.
  • Review focus, border, selected-state, and body-text contrast on Dark, Midnight, and OLED.

docs.title: CI expectations
docs.text:
• Run :composeApp:allTests for shared logic and Compose common tests.
  • Run the screenshot test module's test task and verify no unexpected snapshot changes.
  • Treat intentional visual changes as reviewed snapshots, not silently accepted golden updates.
  • Do not claim desktop runtime or accessibility coverage based solely on Paparazzi snapshots.

docs.title: Development model
docs.text:
Work in the language that owns the capability:

  • Kotlin for application lifecycle, Compose UI, agent orchestration, providers, tools, storage, platform integration, and privileged execution.
  • TypeScript for approved browser-facing UI/integrations, SDKs, and web tooling.

docs.title: Before implementing a cross-language feature
docs.text:
1. Define the use case and owning side.
  2. Specify request, response, and event contracts.
  3. Add JSON Schema and shared positive/negative fixtures.
  4. Define transport, lifecycle, timeout, cancellation, and backpressure.
  5. Define authorization, user confirmation, and audit requirements.
  6. Add contract and security tests on both sides.
  7. Verify independent Kotlin and TypeScript builds.

docs.title: Local checks
docs.text: Use Gradle for Kotlin and pnpm for TypeScript. Neither build should require the other unless a future, reviewed feature explicitly introduces a generated contract artifact.

docs.title: Current limitation
docs.text: The repository currently has schemas and workspace configuration only. There is no bridge, TypeScript runtime feature, plugin SDK, or cross-platform IPC implementation yet.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Node.js 22.15 or newer, below 27
  • pnpm 12.x

The root package manifest pins pnpm to 12.11.2. Use the pinned package manager version to avoid lockfile drift.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
From repository root:

corepack enable
corepack prepare pnpm@12.11.2 --activate
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

If Corepack is unavailable or disabled by the machine policy, install the exact pnpm version using the organization's approved package-management method.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
pnpm frontend:typecheck
pnpm frontend:test
pnpm frontend:format:check
pnpm frontend:check

The current type-check validates the TypeScript Vite/Vitest configuration only. No feature source or test file is intentionally included yet.

docs.title: Isolation guarantees
docs.text:
• Do not add this workspace to Gradle settings.
  • Do not invoke pnpm from Android/Desktop build tasks.
  • Do not add Node.js as an Android runtime dependency.
  • Existing Kotlin/Wasm builds continue to use the existing Kotlin Gradle plugin/toolchain.
  • CI integration should be introduced separately after the initial local workspace is validated.

docs.title: Adding the first feature
docs.text: Before adding a feature, define its runtime target, package boundary, contract, dependencies, threat model, and test plan. Add TypeScript source only within the approved package. Keep Kotlin as the authority for privileged capabilities.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text:
Last verified: 2026-11-03

DORAI AI has a five-way theme picker — System, Light, Dark, OLED and Midnight — exposed in Settings on every platform as a row of switch buttons, one per theme, so the choice is visible at a glance and takes a single tap. The default is System, which follows the operating system's dark/light preference. The other four force a specific theme regardless of system state. Dark uses a soft dark background (#121212) with slightly lighter surfaces (#1E1E1E); OLED flattens the background and the lowest surface tier to pure black (#000000) for users who want to save power on OLED panels; Midnight is a deep-navy dark theme (background #06152E, surfaces #0E2A4D) that keeps the cyan brand accent without going pitch black.

Cards, dialogs, bottom sheets, and menus stay visually lifted in either dark variant because only the lowest surface tiers are affected; container tiers keep their default Material 3 elevation.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• System: isSystemInDarkTheme() decides between the light and dark schemes.
  • Light: forces the Material 3 light scheme.
  • Dark: forces the Material 3 dark scheme. background renders #121212 and surface renders #1E1E1E. surfaceContainer* tiers use their default Material 3 dark values so elevated components remain visible. onBackground / onSurface stay white.
  • OLED: forces dark + pure-black override. background, surface, and surfaceContainerLowest render pure black. The elevated surfaceContainer* tiers are unchanged so cards and menus stay visible against black.
  • Midnight: forces the brand-navy dark scheme. background renders #06152E and surface renders #0E2A4D, with the same cyan accent as the dark theme. It is not the OLED variant, so the adaptive card style stays filled rather than outlined.
  • Material You (Android 12+): the full wallpaper-derived light/dark schemes replace DORAI AI's built-in palettes, so on these devices Dark uses the dynamic dark background and surfaces rather than #121212 / #1E1E1E. When OLED is selected, the black override is layered on top of the dynamic dark scheme so accents and buttons continue to track the wallpaper. Older Android versions and all other platforms use DORAI AI's built-in purple-accented palettes.
  • System bars (Android): status and navigation bars are transparent (edge-to-edge); their icon style follows the resolved theme — Dark, OLED and Midnight always get light icons, Light always gets dark icons, System follows the OS.
  • Reactivity: changing the theme recomposes the theme immediately without an app restart.

The picker exists on every platform because system theme detection is unreliable on some desktop window systems (notably Linux/Wayland), so users there need an explicit override.

docs.title: Component guidance
docs.text:
When adding new surfaces in dark mode, do not bind fills to surface if the element should stand out from the page background with OLED selected — in OLED surface becomes black and the element will be invisible against the background. Use surfaceContainer (or higher) for anything that represents a raised card, pill, or control.

Many cards (settings list items, service/MCP/skill/tool cards, the heartbeat and pending-SMS banners in chat, sandbox file browser rows, dynamic UI cards) use a shared adaptive card style: normally a half-transparent surfaceVariant fill with no border; with OLED selected the fill becomes transparent and a thin outlineVariant border outlines the card instead, keeping the background pure black. New card-like surfaces should reuse this style rather than picking their own fill.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text: File Purpose composeApp/.../ui/Theme.kt DarkColorScheme / LightColorScheme / MidnightColorScheme constants; withBlackBackground() extension that flattens a dark scheme to pure black; adaptive card colors/border/surface helpers that switch to outlined-transparent in OLED composeApp/.../data/AppSettings.kt ThemeMode enum; themeModeFlow / getThemeMode() / setThemeMode() — the persistent setting, with one-time migration from the legacy OLED boolean composeApp/.../App.kt Shared AppContent — observes themeModeFlow, picks lightColorScheme / darkColorScheme / darkColorScheme.withBlackBackground() / MidnightColorScheme based on the selected mode composeApp/.../ui/settings/GeneralSettings.kt Theme mode switch buttons in the General tab androidApp/.../MainActivity.kt Android entry — supplies dynamic-color light/dark schemes; the resolved isDarkTheme (from themeMode + system) drives the system-bar icon style androidApp/.../res/values-night/styles.xml Pre-Compose window background set to #FF121212 to match the default dark frame composeApp/.../iosMain/.../MainViewController.kt iOS entry — uses common App defaults composeApp/.../desktopMain/.../main.kt Desktop entry — uses common App defaults; also configures HiDPI hints and an initial 1280×800 WindowState so the window opens at a usable size on Linux/Wayland

docs.title: Chat & Conversations
docs.text:
Last verified: 2026-11-03

DORAI AI's chat system manages the message history, conversation persistence, file attachments, and speech output. Conversations are service-independent — switching providers does not affect which conversation is loaded or restored. Multiple conversations are persisted and browsable via a history sheet.

docs.title: Conversation
docs.text: A persisted chat session containing an id (UUID), message list, timestamps (createdAt, updatedAt), a title, and a type (chat, heartbeat, or interactive). Conversations are stored in a local database (browser builds use the settings store) and restored across app launches.

docs.title: History
docs.text: The in-memory message list that drives the UI. Each entry has a role: USER, ASSISTANT, TOOL, or TOOL_EXECUTING. History is the source of truth during a session; it is written to a Conversation on save.

docs.title: Conversation Title
docs.text: Auto-derived from the first user message when a conversation is saved for the first time. Truncated to ~50 characters at a word boundary. Once set, titles are not updated.

docs.title: Conversation Lifecycle
docs.text:
• The "current conversation" pointer is persisted across launches: opening the app restores whichever conversation was last active, including an empty new chat the user explicitly started
  • If the persisted pointer references a conversation that no longer exists (or is null because the user started a new chat), the app opens to an empty new chat
  • "New Chat" clears history, unsets the current conversation pointer, and persists the empty state — so an unused new chat survives an app restart
  • A new conversation ID (UUID) is generated on first successful save (after the first assistant response) and immediately becomes the persisted current pointer
  • Conversations are saved after each assistant response
  • Only the most recent 20 exchanges are persisted per chat conversation; heartbeat conversations have a separate, larger cap of 50 messages so longer automation runs are not truncated as aggressively
  • Multiple conversations are persisted — starting a new chat preserves previous conversations
  • Conversations are service-independent — switching services does not affect which conversation is loaded
  • Interactive vs normal chat mode is persisted alongside the current pointer, so an empty interactive chat also survives a restart
  • On the first launch after upgrading from a build that did not persist the current-conversation pointer, a one-time migration pins the most recently updated conversation as the current pointer so the user resumes where they left off
  • On Android, sharing plain text into DORAI AI from another app (the system share sheet) starts a new conversation and puts the shared text in the input field, unsent. The previous conversation stays in history. The user can edit the text or add an instruction, then send as usual. Opening DORAI AI from the launcher or the assist gesture is unchanged; assist still starts an empty new chat

docs.title: Chat History
docs.text:
• A history icon appears in the top bar when saved conversations other than the current one exist
  • Tapping it opens a bottom sheet listing all chat conversations sorted by last updated (newest first)
  • Each item shows the title and formatted date
  • Non-interactive conversations are outlined with a primary-colored border; interactive-mode conversations get an animated gradient border. The active conversation's title is rendered in the primary color (inactive titles use onBackground)
  • Tapping an item loads that conversation and dismisses the sheet
  • Each item has a delete button that defers deletion with a snackbar "Undo" option (~4 seconds) before the conversation is permanently removed. The snackbar appears inside the history sheet so it remains visible while the sheet is open, and the sheet stays open so multiple conversations can be deleted in sequence
  • Deleting the active conversation clears the chat
  • Heartbeat conversations are included in the history list with a "Heartbeat" label badge, and can also be accessed via the heartbeat banner

docs.title: Message Sending
docs.text:
• User message is added to history, then an API call is made via the fallback chain
  • Tool calls are executed inline (TOOL_EXECUTING shown during execution, TOOL result stored after)
  • On success, the conversation is saved
  • On failure, an error is displayed with a retry button
  • Free rate-limit upsell: when the user has no configured services (only Free FAST/EXPERT) and the request fails with a rate-limit, quota-exhausted, or Free proxy capacity error (e.g. “All free providers failed”), the chat shows a special panel instead of the generic error. It explains that Free is rate-limited and shows compact provider chips (icon + name) for free-usage providers (Groq, Cerebras, Gemini, OpenRouter, Ollama Cloud) in a flow layout; tapping a chip opens that provider’s API-key page in the browser. A retry control remains available. The panel is not shown if any non-Free service is already configured.

docs.title: Cancel
docs.text:
• While a request is in progress, a stop button replaces the send button in the input field
  • Clicking stop cancels the ongoing API request and any in-flight tool executions
  • After cancellation, the loading state clears and the send button reappears when typing

docs.title: Retry & Regenerate
docs.text:
• Retry resends the current prompt
  • Regenerate removes all messages after the last user message, then resends

docs.title: File Attachments
docs.text: Multiple files can be attached to a single prompt. Each file is added one at a time via the file picker or drag-and-drop, and appears as a chip below the input. Clicking a chip removes that specific file from the queue. All queued files are cleared after the prompt is sent. Three categories of files are supported:

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
• Attach via file picker or drag-and-drop
  • Compressed to JPEG and Base64-encoded
  • Maximum raw input size: 50 MB; maximum size after compression: 15 MB — rejected with a size error if exceeded
  • Sent as image_url (OpenAI-compatible), image block (Anthropic), or inline_data (Gemini)
  • Not offered on the built-in Free service (its proxy fans out to text-only fallback models that reject multimodal content) or on 1min.AI
  • Also hidden when the active model is known to be text-only (e.g. DeepSeek chat models, GLM text models), even on services that otherwise accept images
  • Shown as a preview thumbnail (max 200dp wide) inside the user message bubble
  • Clicking the thumbnail opens a full-screen viewer with pinch-to-zoom, double-tap to toggle zoom, pan when zoomed, and a close button in the top-right (also dismissable via the Android back button or by tapping the backdrop; desktop has no keyboard shortcut for dismissal)

docs.title: Text files
docs.text:
